outputs.L1:
WASHINGTON (CNN) -- U.S., Turkish, and Iraqi leaders held talks Monday regarding Kurdish rebels’ use of northern Iraq as a launchpad for cross-border attacks into Turkey. Turkish troops patrolled near the Iraqi border on Monday.

President Bush spoke by phone with Turkish Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan, while, separately, two senior figures in Iraq’s national government met with the head of the country’s Kurdish region.

The diplomatic efforts followed Turkish airstrikes on Kurdish separatist targets in northern Iraq on Saturday and Sunday, as well as the previous week.

Bush and Erdogan discussed the threat posed by Kurdish separatist rebels along the Turkish-Iraqi border, the White House confirmed. National Security Council spokesman Gordon Johndroe said the two leaders addressed their shared efforts to combat terrorism and the importance of cooperation among the United States, Turkey, and Iraq in confronting the Kurdistan Workers’ Party, or PKK.

Bush has pledged to help Turkey combat PKK rebels. The PKK has spent two decades fighting for autonomy for Kurds in southeastern Turkey, with some of its attacks launched from northern Iraq. The United States and the European Union designate the group as a terrorist organization.

Last week, Turkey’s ambassador to the United States, Nabi Sensoy, said his country’s operations against Kurdish militant targets in northern Iraq were based on intelligence provided by the United States.

In the Iraqi Kurdish city of Sulaimaniya, Iraqi President Jalal Talabani, who is Kurdish, and Vice President Tariq al-Hashimi, who is Sunni Arab, met with Kurdish Regional Government President Massoud Barzani.

Iraqi Kurdish officials, while critical of the PKK, have denounced Turkey’s bombing campaign. Last week, Barzani declined to meet with visiting U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice in protest over the attacks.

“We have vehemently condemned the bombardment. The bombing targeted safe and secure areas and innocent people. Several people were either killed or wounded,” Barzani said Monday at a press conference with the other officials. “We held consultations with President Jalal Talabani, and we will continue our consultations with other concerned parties to put an end to these aggressions and to the shelling of villages.”

The three Iraqi officials also addressed national unity. They signed a “memorandum of understanding” to further deepen relations among their three parties: Talabani’s Patriotic Union of Kurdistan, Barzani’s Kurdistan Democratic Party, and al-Hashimi’s Iraqi Islamic Party, a Sunni Arab entity.

CNN’s Kathleen Koch, Talia Kayali, and Mohammed Tawfeeq contributed to this report.

WASHINGTON (CNN) — On Monday, leaders from the United States, Turkey and Iraq engaged in discussions over Kurdish rebels who have been using northern Iraq as a base for attacks across the border into Turkey.

Turkish forces were seen patrolling near the Iraqi frontier on Monday. President Bush spoke by telephone with Turkish Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan. In a separate meeting, two senior officials from Iraq’s national government held talks with the leader of the Kurdish region in Iraq.

The diplomatic activity followed Turkish airstrikes against Kurdish separatist positions in northern Iraq on Saturday and Sunday, as well as during the previous week.

The White House confirmed that Bush and Erdogan discussed the threat posed by Kurdish separatist militants along the border between Turkey and Iraq. Gordon Johndroe, spokesman for the National Security Council, said the two leaders talked about shared efforts to combat terrorism and stressed the need for the United States, Turkey and Iraq to cooperate in dealing with the Kurdistan Workers’ Party, known as the PKK.

Bush has promised to support Turkey in its fight against PKK militants. The PKK has waged a 20-year campaign seeking autonomy for Kurds in southeastern Turkey, and some of its attacks have been carried out from bases in northern Iraq. Both the United States and the European Union classify the PKK as a terrorist organization.

The previous week, Turkey’s ambassador to Washington, Nabi Sensoy, said Turkish operations against Kurdish militant targets in northern Iraq had relied on intelligence supplied by the United States.

In Sulaimaniya, a city in Iraqi Kurdistan, Iraqi President Jalal Talabani, who is Kurdish, and Vice President Tariq al-Hashimi, a Sunni Arab, met with Massoud Barzani, president of the Kurdish Regional Government.

Although Iraqi Kurdish officials have criticized the PKK, they have also condemned Turkey’s bombing campaign. The week before, Barzani refused to meet visiting U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice as a protest against the attacks.

“We have strongly condemned the bombardment,” Barzani said Monday during a news conference with the other officials. “The bombing struck safe and stable areas and innocent civilians. A number of people were killed or injured.”

He added, “We have consulted with President Jalal Talabani, and we will continue discussions with other relevant parties in order to stop these aggressions and end the shelling of villages.”

The three Iraqi leaders also addressed the issue of national unity. They signed a “memorandum of understanding” intended to strengthen ties among their three political groups: Talabani’s Patriotic Union of Kurdistan, Barzani’s Kurdistan Democratic Party and al-Hashimi’s Iraqi Islamic Party, a Sunni Arab organization.

CNN’s Kathleen Koch, Talia Kayali and Mohammed Tawfeeq contributed to this report.

U.S., Turkish and Iraqi leaders held talks aimed at addressing the long-running problem of Kurdish PKK rebels using northern Iraq as a base for attacks inside Turkey, as all sides sought to manage tensions following Turkish airstrikes on suspected rebel targets.

The discussions focused on developing a coordinated diplomatic and counterterrorism approach to the PKK, which Turkey considers a major security threat. Turkish officials have repeatedly accused the group of operating from mountainous areas in northern Iraq and crossing the border to carry out attacks on Turkish forces and civilians. In response, Turkey has carried out military strikes against positions it says are linked to the rebels.

U.S. officials expressed support for Turkey’s efforts to defend itself against the PKK, while also emphasizing the need for cooperation among Ankara, Baghdad and authorities in Iraq’s Kurdish region. Washington has sought to prevent the issue from further destabilizing northern Iraq, an area that has often been central to broader regional security concerns.

At the same time, the Turkish airstrikes have angered many Iraqi Kurds, who view the bombings as a violation of Iraqi territory and a threat to civilian security. Kurdish officials in northern Iraq have warned that repeated military action could inflame local resentment and complicate relations with Turkey, even as they face pressure to curb PKK activity in areas under their influence.

The talks highlighted the delicate balance facing all three governments: Turkey wants stronger action against PKK militants, Iraq is concerned about sovereignty and stability, and the United States is trying to support a key ally while avoiding a wider regional confrontation. The outcome of these discussions could shape future cooperation on border security, intelligence sharing and efforts to reduce violence along the Turkey-Iraq frontier.

The issue remains a major test of regional diplomacy. Continued attacks by the PKK, further Turkish military operations, or a breakdown in coordination among the parties could raise tensions and undermine stability in northern Iraq. **Bush, Erdogan discuss PKK rebels after Turkish strikes in northern Iraq**

**WASHINGTON (CNN-style report)** — President George W. Bush and Turkish Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan discussed Turkey’s campaign against Kurdish PKK rebels in northern Iraq following a series of Turkish airstrikes that drew sharp criticism from Iraqi Kurdish leaders, officials said.

The talks came after Turkish warplanes targeted suspected positions of the Kurdistan Workers’ Party, or PKK, in mountainous areas of northern Iraq, where the group has maintained bases used to launch attacks across the border into Turkey.

Turkey considers the PKK a terrorist organization, as do the United States and the European Union. The group has waged a decades-long insurgency against the Turkish state, and Ankara has repeatedly demanded stronger action against PKK fighters operating from Iraqi territory.

Bush, who has sought to balance support for NATO ally Turkey with the need to preserve stability in Iraq, previously pledged improved intelligence-sharing with Ankara. U.S. officials have said Washington recognizes Turkey’s right to defend itself but has urged coordination with Iraqi authorities and steps to avoid civilian casualties.

Turkish officials said the air operations were aimed solely at PKK targets. “Our struggle is with the terrorist organization,” Erdogan has said in past remarks, insisting that Turkey does not seek confrontation with Iraq’s Kurdish population.

But leaders in Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdish region reacted angrily to the strikes, saying the attacks violated Iraqi sovereignty and threatened civilians in remote border villages.

Massoud Barzani, president of the Kurdistan Regional Government at the time, condemned the Turkish military action and warned against turning the region into a battlefield.

“We do not accept the violation of Iraq’s sovereignty,” Barzani said, according to Kurdish officials. He also warned that the Kurdish regional authorities would not remain silent if civilians were harmed, saying the region’s people had the right to defend themselves.

Kurdish officials said some residents fled villages near the bombing areas, though reports of casualties and damage were difficult to verify independently because of the rugged terrain.

The Iraqi central government also objected to unilateral military action on its territory, while urging the PKK not to use Iraq as a staging ground for attacks on neighboring countries.

The dispute underscored the fragile diplomacy surrounding northern Iraq: Turkey fears PKK safe havens along its border; Iraqi Kurds oppose Turkish military incursions; Baghdad insists on sovereignty; and Washington has tried to prevent a wider conflict that could destabilize one of Iraq’s relatively calmer regions.

U.S. officials have pressed for a three-way approach among Washington, Ankara and Baghdad, including intelligence cooperation and political pressure on the PKK. But Turkey has maintained that if militants continue to attack Turkish soldiers and civilians, it will act militarily when necessary.

The PKK insurgency has killed tens of thousands of people since it began in 1984. While the group’s presence in northern Iraq has long been a source of tension, Turkish cross-border airstrikes brought renewed urgency to diplomatic efforts to contain the conflict.

counterfactuals.output:
**Turkey Expands Campaign Against Kurdish Rebels in Northern Iraq as U.S.-Turkey Coordination Deepens and Baghdad Faces Pressure Over Bombings**

**ANKARA / BAGHDAD / WASHINGTON —** Turkey has intensified its cross-border campaign against Kurdish militants based in northern Iraq, carrying out air and artillery strikes against suspected positions of the Kurdistan Workers’ Party, or PKK, while pressing both Iraq and the United States for greater cooperation against the group.

The campaign has unfolded amid renewed diplomatic activity involving Ankara, Washington and Baghdad, including U.S.-Turkey security coordination against the PKK and an Iraqi memorandum of understanding aimed at addressing Turkish security concerns. But the operations have also triggered criticism from Iraqi officials, Kurdish political figures and rights advocates who accuse Turkey of violating Iraqi sovereignty and endangering civilians in mountainous border areas.

The PKK, which has waged an insurgency against the Turkish state for decades, is designated as a terrorist organization by Turkey, the United States and the European Union. The group maintains camps and logistical networks in rugged areas of northern Iraq, particularly around the Qandil Mountains and other zones near the Turkish border. Ankara says those bases are used to plan and launch attacks inside Turkey and against Turkish forces deployed in Iraq.

Turkish officials have described the latest operations as part of a sustained effort to dismantle PKK infrastructure beyond Turkey’s borders. The Turkish military has conducted repeated airstrikes, drone attacks and ground incursions in northern Iraq in recent years, establishing a network of outposts in some border areas. Ankara argues that the Iraqi state has been unable or unwilling to remove PKK fighters from its territory and says Turkey has the right to act in self-defense.

Iraqi leaders, however, have faced mounting domestic pressure over Turkish bombardments. Officials in Baghdad and the Kurdistan Regional Government, or KRG, have at times condemned strikes that they say hit near villages, farms and civilian infrastructure. Residents in affected areas have reported displacement, damage to livestock and orchards, and fear of returning to mountain communities caught between Turkish forces and PKK fighters.

The political sensitivity is acute for Iraq’s federal government, which must balance relations with Turkey — a major trading partner and upstream water power — with demands to defend Iraqi sovereignty. Turkey is also a key energy and transit neighbor for both Baghdad and the semi-autonomous Kurdish region.

In response to Ankara’s security demands, Iraqi officials have taken steps to formalize cooperation. Iraqi leaders have signed a memorandum of understanding intended to improve coordination over security along the border and address the presence of armed groups operating from Iraqi territory. While details have not been fully publicized in some accounts, the agreement is widely seen as part of a broader effort by Baghdad to prevent northern Iraq from becoming a flashpoint in relations with Turkey.

The memorandum has drawn criticism from some Iraqi and Kurdish factions, who say Baghdad risks appearing to legitimize Turkish military operations while failing to secure firm guarantees against civilian harm. Others argue that the PKK’s entrenched presence has exposed the region to repeated attacks and given Turkey an opening to expand its military footprint.

For the United States, the issue presents a delicate diplomatic balancing act. Washington regards the PKK as a terrorist organization and has long supported Turkey’s right to defend itself against PKK attacks. At the same time, U.S. policy in Iraq and Syria has relied heavily on Kurdish partners, particularly Syrian Kurdish-led forces that Turkey views as closely linked to the PKK. That has produced years of tension between Ankara and Washington.

U.S.-Turkey cooperation against the PKK has included intelligence sharing, security consultations and joint diplomatic messaging. American officials have repeatedly stated that the PKK should not be allowed to use Iraqi territory as a base for attacks on Turkey. Washington has also encouraged closer coordination among Turkey, Iraq and the KRG to reduce the risk of escalation and civilian casualties.

Turkish officials have pressed the United States to take a tougher line not only against the PKK in Iraq but also against Kurdish groups in Syria that Ankara identifies as part of the same militant network. U.S. officials distinguish between the PKK and their Syrian partners in the fight against the Islamic State, a distinction Turkey rejects.

The latest escalation comes as Turkey seeks to establish what officials have called a permanent security belt along its southern borders with Iraq and Syria. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and senior defense officials have signaled that operations will continue until PKK routes, shelters and command points are eliminated. Turkish media, often citing defense ministry sources, have reported strikes on caves, depots and training sites, though independent verification in remote mountain areas is difficult.

The PKK has historically used northern Iraq’s mountainous terrain to evade Turkish pressure, shifting between camps and taking advantage of gaps among Iraqi federal forces, KRG security units and local administrations. The group’s presence has also strained Kurdish politics in Iraq, where the dominant Kurdistan Democratic Party has tense relations with the PKK, while other Kurdish factions have urged restraint and dialogue.

Analysts say the memorandum of understanding may mark a significant step if it leads to sustained Iraqi action restricting PKK movement, financing and recruitment. But they caution that implementation will be difficult. Baghdad has limited control over parts of the north, and the KRG itself is divided politically and institutionally. Any move against PKK networks could also provoke backlash in areas where the group has sympathizers or where residents oppose Turkish military activity.

Humanitarian groups have called for greater transparency from all sides. They say civilian communities in northern Iraq have borne the consequences of a conflict in which they have little control. Some villages near the border have been partially or fully abandoned over years of fighting, while farmers say access to grazing lands and orchards has become increasingly dangerous.

Turkey insists that it takes precautions to avoid civilians and targets only militants. Critics counter that repeated strikes near populated areas create unacceptable risks and that the presence of Turkish bases inside Iraq has become a source of instability.

The Iraqi government has sought to frame its latest diplomacy as an assertion of state authority rather than a concession to Ankara. Iraqi officials have said that armed groups operating outside state control cannot be allowed to undermine relations with neighboring countries. At the same time, they have called for respect for Iraq’s sovereignty and for security arrangements to be handled through official channels.

The dispute reflects the broader regional complexity surrounding Kurdish armed movements, Turkish security policy and Iraq’s fragile sovereignty. For Ankara, the PKK remains one of its top national-security threats. For Baghdad, the challenge is to prevent Iraq from being used as a battlefield by outside powers or non-state armed groups. For Washington, cooperation with Turkey against the PKK must be managed alongside its wider commitments in Iraq and Syria.

As military operations continue, the memorandum and U.S.-Turkey coordination may help reduce diplomatic friction, but they are unlikely to end the conflict quickly. The PKK’s long-established presence in northern Iraq, Turkey’s determination to pursue it across borders, and Iraqi unease over foreign military action suggest the region will remain a volatile front in a conflict that has spanned four decades.
